subject: Rendering ggplots with a large underlying data.frame

messages.author: 9c9b5f9c6aaa025d
messages.subject: Rendering ggplots with a large underlying data.frame
parts:
Hi,
I am not sure if this is better suited for the ggplot2 mailing list, but I will try here first since the use case is really tied to shiny. 

I am trying to plot a huge data.frame that takes up to 10 seconds to render. It becomes tiresome to have to wait 10 seconds every time I change an input parameter. My question: is there a way to "pre-render" the ggplots? 

For example, based on the inputs I have, there are N possible plots that could be created. Can I somehow pre-render all N images so that when the reactive input is resolved, all that needs to happen is a simple lookup instead of the full rendering of the ggplot? That way I can spend the computation time before launching the server (e.g., while I sleep) and the interface with shiny is very quick (e.g., when I interact with my boss).

Many thanks,
Doug

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Rendering ggplots with a large underlying data.frame
parts:
Hi Doug -

If you can pre-render your plots when the app starts, you might be able to come up with something that will work. But if you need to re-render the plots in response to user input, the single-threaded nature of R will cause blocking when the plots are re-rendered (although you might be able to speed things up with something like mclapply).

So lets assume that you can pre-render all the plots at the beginning. This imposes the limitation that the plots have to be a predetermined size; they can't respond to changes in the browser window.

I have a partial solution -- but you would need to figure out how to do the following:
  png('myfile.png')
  {
    ## Put some code here that will read an existing png file and output it
  }
  dev.off()

... because this renderPlot() wraps your block of code with the png() and dev.off() -- and, importantly, it decides the name of the file. As far as I know, there's no function that will do that. Another way to go is to make your own function based on renderPlot that can do this.

At any rate, here's the skeleton code that I came up with (it needs that critical part filled in):

downloader::source_url("https://gist.github.com/wch/5003044/raw/aa4dbbca0023e29a629386b1ee9a5d27b2e37362/shinyserialize.r")

shinyRun(
# --------------------------------------
`global.R` = quote({
  min_bins <- 5
  max_bins <- 20
}),
# --------------------------------------
`ui.R` = quote({
  shinyUI(
    pageWithSidebar(               
        headerPanel(""),
        sidebarPanel(
          sliderInput("bins", "Bins", min=min_bins, max=max_bins, value=10)
        ),
        mainPanel(                 
          plotOutput("outplot")
        )
      )
  )
}),
# --------------------------------------
`server.R` = quote({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(png)

  shinyServer(function(input, output) {
    outfile_prefix <- tempfile()

    prerender <- function() {
      set.seed(456)
      dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(400))

      p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x))

      for (bins in min_bins:max_bins) {
        filename <- paste(outfile_prefix, "-", bins, ".png", sep="")
        png(filename, width=400, height=400)
        print(p + geom_histogram(colour="black", fill="white",
                                 binwidth=diff(range(dat$x))/bins))
        dev.off()
      }
    }

    # Render all the plots when the user connects to the session
    prerender()

    output$outplot <- renderPlot({
      filename <- paste(outfile_prefix, "-", input$bins, ".png", sep="")
      
      ## Do something here that would read the saved file and write it out.
      ## It must work when this block of code is surrounded by png() and dev.off()

    }, width=400, height=400)
  })
})
)



Yet another option: If the images are rendered before the app even starts, then you could do something like this:
* Store the images in www/
* use renderText() to generate raw HTML that contains an <img> tag pointing to the selected image
* display it with htmlOutput()

You could even go further in this direction, and not use Shiny for this part -- you could do it with just Javascript. Ryan Mears had an example that did something like this. See this thread for more information: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/shiny-discuss/ITFUwvYE-f8/Pam8vqpxFQQJ

-Winston
